doc.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

chapter: Tuba in jazz history and technique
title: Why the tuba fell out of use: Milt Hinton and volume
summary: Hinton says the tuba was too country; Stewart explains the physical demands of playing a four feel at big band volume and using a mic on his bell.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Was it partly volume and partly just the physical limitations of the instruments that you couldn’t walk all night?
I don’t know. I don’t really know. I was on the Spike Lee record date, it was “Jungle Fever” or it was “No More Some Blues.”

“Mo Better Blues” right. And during the record date Milt Hinton was on the date. And I asked him, I said since you were there and I know you migrated to Chicago in the late teens when you were like ten or eleven years old, why did they stop using the tuba? And his answer, coming from a person who was not a tuba player, was, “Well you know the tuba was like a country instrument. It was an instrument for parades and stuff like that. And we were moving north. We were moving up to the city. And it just wasn’t hip enough. You know nobody wanted a tuba, they wanted to hear upright bass. It was like more urban and more city-fied.” That’s what he said. Now as a tuba player I know full well if a tuba player had to sit back there and play in one of those big bands of the thirties where in fact it was in four and you have to play to the volume of 15 cats playing horns, a

drummer, a guitar player, who quite often had, by that time they were starting to be amplified, the guitar, there’s no way you could do that. I mean I started out with Arthur Blythe in his quartet, quintet. And I can’t tell you how many cuts I got trying to maintain that thing without an amplifier with a contemporary drummer. And still we weren’t playing as loud as one of those big bands. Trying to maintain a four feel and that contemporary style of playing, the bass function. And I mean swollen lips and ice packs and cuts and so forth. And I had, because it’s just very difficult to do physically. It’s very difficult to do. And to play to that volume inevitably what happens is you start getting tired. And when you start getting tired you start slowing down. You see? And that’s why I know those bass players, the tuba players could not have done that, and those guys went out on the road for how many weeks at a time? There’s no way his chops could have handled that. No way. So that’s one of the reasons when I’m doing that function I have a microphone on my bell so when I’m playing that function I’m playing like I’m sitting in my room practicing. And so I let the — in New York, the electric company is called Con Edison, I let Con Edison do the rest of it. I let Con Edison come up to the level of that sizzle cymbal that’s ringing all the time.
Because a drummer hits one of those sizzle cymbals — bamm — so all my notes are wiped for the next ten seconds while that sizzle — [scats].
